title: Elders for Crete and Teachers Who Must Be Silenced
summary: Paul greets Titus with a full description of his apostleship, rooted in God's promise of eternal life made before time began. He reminds Titus that he left him in Crete to put the churches in order and appoint elders in every town, and he lists the qualities an elder or overseer must have, above all a blameless life and a firm hold on sound teaching. He then describes rebellious teachers, many from a Jewish background, who upset whole households for gain, and tells Titus to rebuke them sharply.
story: Paul and Titus had evidently worked together on Crete, and when Paul moved on he left Titus to finish the task. This chapter tells us what was unfinished: the churches had no appointed leaders, and teachers were spreading myths and human commands. The remedy has two sides. First, appoint the right people, whose lives and teaching can be trusted. Second, silence those who are doing harm. The chapter parallels 1 Timothy 3, but its setting is younger churches and its tone blunter. Behind it lies a conviction that runs through the whole letter: what people believe shows up in how they live, and what they do shows what they really believe (verse 16).
historical:
Crete had been part of a Roman province, joined with Cyrene in North Africa, since the first century BC. It had several cities, and there were Jewish communities on the island; the Jewish writer Philo mentions Jews in Crete, and Cretan Jews were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:11). Acts records no mission on Crete, only Paul's voyage past its southern coast as a prisoner (Acts 27:7-13). Scholars who hold that Paul wrote the letter place the mission on Crete after his release from his first Roman imprisonment, in the early 60s AD; scholars who see the letter as the work of a later follower of Paul regard the setting as part of its portrayal of Paul and date it later, often between about AD 80 and 110.

The false teachers are described as “those of the circumcision” (verse 10), that is, Jewish believers or Jews who insisted on elements of the law, and their teaching involved “Jewish myths” and “the commands of men” (verse 14), apparently including rules about purity (verse 15). The details are not given, but the pattern resembles the teaching in Ephesus described in 1 Timothy: speculation, ritual rules, and a mercenary motive. Appointing elders in each town followed Paul's practice from his earliest mission (Acts 14:23).
cultural:
Paul quotes a line from “one of their own prophets” (verse 12). Ancient tradition, reported by Clement of Alexandria among others, attributed it to Epimenides, a Cretan seer and poet of about the sixth century BC; the opening words also appear in the Hellenistic poet Callimachus. The saying reflected a widespread Greek stereotype: Cretans claimed that the tomb of Zeus was on their island, which other Greeks regarded as a lie, since Zeus was immortal, and the Greeks even formed a verb from the island's name meaning to lie. Paul uses the quotation with some irony, turning a Cretan's own words against the false teachers. He does not say every Cretan is a liar; his target is the teachers and those influenced by them, and his goal is that they become sound in the faith (verse 13).

The qualifications for elders assume the household structure of the Roman world, where a man was expected to govern his household, including children and slaves, and where a household's disorder reflected on its head. An overseer is called “God's steward” (verse 7), using the word for the household manager, often a trusted slave or freedman, who ran a wealthy estate on the owner's behalf. The image fits the church as God's household: leaders do not own it; they manage it for him.
literary: The opening greeting (verses 1-4) is the longest of any Pauline letter except Romans, and it packs in the letter's key themes: faith, knowledge of the truth, godliness, the hope of eternal life, God's promise, and God as Savior. Verses 5-9 give the qualifications of elders. The list is built largely from negatives and positives: five things an overseer must not be (verse 7), six things he must be (verse 8), and one thing he must hold (verse 9). Verses 10-16 describe the opponents, with a quotation (verse 12), a command (verse 13), a principle (verse 15), and a verdict (verse 16). The word for “sound” or healthy (verses 9 and 13) ties the elder's teaching to the healing Titus must bring to the opponents. The terms elder and overseer are used interchangeably in verses 5 and 7.

outline.t: Greeting: Paul's apostleship and the hope of eternal life
Appoint elders in every town: blameless in family life
The overseer as God's steward: character and sound teaching
Rebellious teachers who must be silenced and rebuked
Pure and defiled: professing God but denying him by deeds

doctrines.note: Churches need recognized leaders, appointed with care, whose lives are blameless and who hold firmly to “the faithful word as it was taught” (verse 9). The elder's two tasks are to encourage by sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it.

God is the one “who cannot lie” (verse 2), and his promise of eternal life was made before time began. The reliability of the gospel rests on the truthfulness of God, a pointed contrast with a culture known for liars.
“To the pure, all things are pure” (verse 15). Echoing Jesus' teaching that defilement comes from within (Mark 7:15-23), Paul locates impurity in the mind and conscience, not in foods or rituals.

words.note: Apseudēs, free from falsehood, found only here in the New Testament. God is the one “who cannot lie” (verse 2). Set against the Cretan saying of verse 12, the contrast is sharp: the island may be known for lying, but the God of the gospel is not.
Epidiorthoō, to set right further or put in order what remains. It suggests correcting or completing work already begun. Titus is not founding the churches of Crete but finishing their organization.
Oikonomos, a household manager or steward. The overseer is “God's steward” (verse 7): not the owner of the church but a servant entrusted with managing it for its true master, and accountable to him.

Pistos, faithful or believing. In verse 6 the elder's children are described with this word, which can mean either believers or faithful in the sense of trustworthy and well behaved. The translation affects how strict the qualification is, as the hard question below explains.

christ: The opening verses root Paul's ministry in God's saving plan, and they give the title Savior both to God (verse 3) and to Christ Jesus (verse 4). The promise of eternal life was made “before time began” (verse 2) and has now been made evident in the proclamation of the gospel, which is the message of Christ. The qualifications for elders reflect the character of Christ, the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep and who was not violent, greedy, or quick-tempered. Paul's principle that “To the pure, all things are pure” (verse 15) applies Jesus' own teaching that what defiles a person comes from the heart (Mark 7:18-23). The chapter's final verdict, that some profess God but deny him by their actions, echoes Jesus' warning that not everyone who says Lord, Lord will enter the kingdom (Matthew 7:21).

hard.q: What do the elder qualifications require about marriage, children, and gender?
hard.a:
Several phrases here are debated. The phrase “the husband of but one wife” (verse 6) has been read as requiring marital faithfulness (literally a one-woman man), forbidding polygamy, forbidding remarriage after divorce, or requiring that an elder be married. The phrase “children who are believers” can also be translated faithful children, and interpreters divide over whether an elder's children must profess faith, which is ultimately beyond a parent's control, or must be well behaved and not open to charges of wildness, as the rest of the verse suggests.

Whether elders must be men is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ. The complementarian reading holds that the office of elder is reserved for qualified men. It notes that the qualifications are stated in male terms, that the elder's role of teaching and refuting (verse 9) corresponds to the authority 1 Timothy 2:12 restricts, and that Paul's instructions reflect a pattern grounded in creation, not merely in custom. The egalitarian reading holds that Paul describes the normal case in a patriarchal society without forbidding women from leading in other settings. It notes that the phrase about one wife addresses faithfulness rather than gender, that Paul elsewhere names women as coworkers, a deacon (Romans 16:1), and apostles (Romans 16:7), and that the household expectations assumed here belong to Roman social structures that the gospel was already beginning to transform. Readers should weigh both main readings in their strongest form.

questions: Most of the elder's qualifications concern character rather than skill. Why might trustworthy character matter more than talent in leading a church?
Paul says some “profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.” Where might your actions deny what you say you believe?
How can a church correct false teaching firmly, as Paul commands, without becoming harsh or suspicious of everyone?
